landscape: Environmental and climate politics data fall into five families. Governance data record international agreements and participation (the International Environmental Agreements Database ENV-001, TREND ENV-002, TFDD ENV-003, UNFCCC attendance and youth-participation data ENV-006/007). They also record national pledges and their transparency (Climate Watch NDC content ENV-009, NDC Explorer ENV-010, Climate Action Tracker ENV-012, Net Zero Tracker ENV-013, the Transparency Adherence Index ENV-008).

Law and policy data code what governments adopt: climate legislation (Climate Change Laws of the World ENV-017), litigation (Sabin Center ENV-018), policy inventories (Climate Policy Database ENV-023, IEA Policies ENV-026, GCCMPD ENV-027), policy stringency (OECD CAPMF ENV-024 and its predecessor EPS ENV-025). Further datasets cover carbon pricing and subsidies (World Carbon Pricing Database ENV-029, World Bank dashboard ENV-030, OECD Effective Carbon Rates ENV-033, EU ETS data ENV-034, fossil-fuel subsidies ENV-032). Climate finance and environmental aid are covered by OECD Rio-marker data (ENV-037), Climate Funds Update (ENV-038) and PLAID (ENV-041).

Outcome data measure emissions, energy and environmental conditions. They include national inventories (EDGAR ENV-043, PRIMAP-hist ENV-044, the Global Carbon Budget ENV-045, Climate Watch ENV-047, UNFCCC submissions ENV-048), facility and asset estimates (Climate TRACE ENV-049, EPA GHGRP ENV-105), energy statistics (EIA, IEA, Energy Institute, UNSD, Ember: ENV-052 to 056) and land use (Global Forest Change ENV-060, MapBiomas ENV-061). Composite indices summarise performance and vulnerability (EPI ENV-066, ND-GAIN ENV-073, INFORM ENV-074, WorldRiskIndex ENV-075).

Political behavior and conflict data cover climate opinion (Yale Climate Opinion Maps ENV-080, Climate Change in the American Mind ENV-081, the Meta-Yale international survey ENV-084) and parties and legislators (Policlim ENV-088, LCV scorecard ENV-090; party positions also in CHES and MARPOR). They also cover protest and environmental justice (Carnegie Climate Protest Tracker ENV-091, EJAtlas ENV-092, EJScreen and CEJST, both withdrawn in 2025), water conflict (ENV-093/094) and disasters (EM-DAT ENV-095, GDIS ENV-096). Corporate ESG ratings (ENV-112 to 116) are commercial and diverge sharply across vendors.

core.text: The International Environmental Agreements Database records multilateral and bilateral environmental agreements, their texts, amendments and state membership, covering over 1,100 multilateral and about 1,500 bilateral agreements. Founded by Ronald Mitchell at the University of Oregon, it is now hosted by Universite Laval (co-directed with Jean-Frederic Morin). It is often used in treaty-participation and regime-design research. Bilateral agreements are less complete than multilateral ones. Because files are updated continuously, users should archive the extract they analyse.

Climate Change Laws of the World, maintained by the Grantham Research Institute at LSE with Climate Policy Radar technology, lists more than 9,000 national climate laws, policies and UNFCCC submissions for all UNFCCC parties. It is a common source for counting and classifying climate legislation. It is national only, uses machine translation and reports no inter-coder reliability. Coverage is better for recent laws and well-covered countries. Climate litigation now sits in the Sabin Center database (ENV-018).

The Climate Policy Database (NewClimate Institute with Wageningen and PBL) records about 6,700 climate policies in 198 jurisdictions with roughly 28 coded attributes, released in versioned Zenodo snapshots. Coverage is comprehensive for only 42 countries, so policy counts elsewhere partly reflect research effort. Counts also do not measure stringency; for that, OECD's CAPMF (ENV-024; 130 policy variables for 50 countries and the EU, 1990-2023) is the better source.

The Global Carbon Budget's national fossil CO2 data (Global Carbon Project) give annual emissions from 1750 to the latest year, with consumption-based series, and are archived by version on Zenodo. EDGAR (ENV-043) offers a model-based alternative covering all greenhouse gases from 1970, and PRIMAP-hist (ENV-044) a composite series from 1750. They are common dependent variables in emissions research. The Global Carbon Budget covers CO2 only and picks the best source per country; EDGAR's latest year is a fast-track extrapolation and can differ from countries' own inventories.

The Environmental Performance Index (Yale and Columbia CIESIN) scores 177 countries on 47 indicators in its 2026 edition and is a widely used summary of national environmental performance. Indicators, sources and weights change every edition (58 indicators in 2024, 40 in 2022). The producers state that scores from different editions must not be compared or stacked into a panel; each edition offers only a baseline score and indicator series. Its predecessor, the Environmental Sustainability Index (ENV-067), ended in 2005.

choosing: For treaty participation use IEADB (ENV-001); for environmental provisions in trade agreements use TREND (ENV-002); for river treaties and water events use TFDD (ENV-003).

For climate laws use CCLW (ENV-017) for counts and texts, the Climate Policy Database (ENV-023) for policy-level attributes, and OECD CAPMF (ENV-024) for comparable stringency scores; EPS (ENV-025) ends in 2020.

For emissions, report results with more than one inventory: the Global Carbon Budget or PRIMAP-hist for long CO2 series, EDGAR for all gases since 1970, and UNFCCC submissions (ENV-048) when the analysis concerns what governments themselves report.

For carbon pricing, the World Carbon Pricing Database (ENV-029) gives sector-level coverage and prices to 2020; the World Bank dashboard (ENV-030) and ICAP (ENV-031) are current but descriptive; OECD Effective Carbon Rates (ENV-033) combine taxes and permit prices.

For environmental performance, use EPI indicator series rather than ranks for over-time work; for climate vulnerability use ND-GAIN (ENV-073) for long annual series and INFORM (ENV-074) for humanitarian risk.

For U.S. climate opinion use Yale's small-area estimates (ENV-080) for geography and CCAM microdata (ENV-081) for individual-level analysis; for cross-national opinion use the Meta-Yale survey aggregates (ENV-084) or the World Risk Poll (ENV-085).

For disasters, EM-DAT (ENV-095) is the global event list (registration required) and GDIS (ENV-096) geocodes it to 2018; U.S. studies can use FEMA declarations (ENV-101) and NOAA Storm Events (ENV-100).
gaps: No maintained dataset codes green parties or environmental NGOs cross-nationally; party climate positions rely on manifesto coding (Policlim, MARPOR, CHES) and PARTYCLIM has not yet released data.
Policy datasets are dense for OECD countries and thin elsewhere: CAPMF covers 50 countries, and the Climate Policy Database is comprehensive for only 42.
Implementation and enforcement are rarely measured: most policy indices code adoption and design, not compliance, outside the U.S. EPA enforcement data.
Several U.S. federal tools were withdrawn in 2025 (EJScreen, CEJST, NOAA billion-dollar disasters), leaving researchers with archived copies and non-governmental continuations.
Composite indices (EPI, CCPI, Climate Risk Index) change methods between editions, so long comparable series must be rebuilt from their component indicators.
